claim: Massed synchronised neuronal firing is detrimental to information processing.
source: Massed synchronised neuronal firing is detrimental to information processing.
evidence: This is stated as a foundational premise in the abstract and introduction, drawing on established neuroscience knowledge about signal-to-noise ratios.

claim: When networks of task-irrelevant neurons fire in unison, they mask the signal generated by task-critical neurons.
source: When networks of task-irrelevant neurons fire in unison, they mask the signal generated by task-critical neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical principle in the abstract, based on established understanding of neural noise.

claim: Synchronisation can contribute to alpha/beta (8–30 Hz) oscillations on a macroscopic level.
source: On a macroscopic level, such synchronisation can contribute to alpha/beta (8–30 Hz) oscillations.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical connection in the abstract, linking microscopic neural synchrony to macroscopic oscillations.

claim: Twenty-one participants completed an associative memory task while undergoing simultaneous EEG-fMRI recordings.
source: Twenty-one participants completed an associative memory task while undergoing simultaneous EEG-fMRI recordings.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental design in the abstract.

claim: As post-stimulus alpha/beta power decreased, stimulus-specific information increased.
source: When correlating this metric with concurrently-recorded alpha/beta power, we found a significant negative correlation which indicated that as post-stimulus alpha/beta power decreased, stimulus-specific information increased.
evidence: This is the main finding reported in the abstract, supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The negative correlation between alpha/beta power and stimulus-specific information was found in three unique tasks: visual perception, auditory perception, and visual memory retrieval.
source: Critically, we found this effect in three unique tasks: visual perception, auditory perception, and visual memory retrieval, indicating that this phenomenon transcends both stimulus modality and cognitive task.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key finding, supported by data from multiple experimental conditions.

claim: The phenomenon of alpha/beta power decreases tracking stimulus-specific information transcends both stimulus modality and cognitive task.
source: Critically, we found this effect in three unique tasks: visual perception, auditory perception, and visual memory retrieval, indicating that this phenomenon transcends both stimulus modality and cognitive task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings stated in the abstract, based on the observation across multiple conditions.

claim: Alpha/beta power decreases parametrically track the fidelity of both externally-presented and internally-generated stimulus-specific information represented within the cortex.
source: These results indicate that alpha/beta power decreases parametrically track the fidelity of both externally-presented and internally-generated stimulus-specific information represented within the cortex.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, based on the experimental findings.

claim: Neural oscillations are rhythmic fluctuations in neuronal activity that can be observed throughout the brain at frequencies ranging from 0.05 Hz to 500 Hz.
source: Neuronal activity fluctuates rhythmically over time. Often referred to as 'neural oscillations', these rhythmic fluctuations can be observed throughout the brain at frequencies ranging from 0.05 Hz to 500 Hz (Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Alpha and beta frequencies (8–12 Hz; 13–30 Hz) dominate when recording from the human scalp.
source: When recording from the human scalp, it is the alpha and beta frequencies (8–12 Hz; 13–30 Hz) that dominate.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the introduction.

claim: Engaging in a cognitive task produces a large reduction in alpha/beta power.
source: Alpha/beta activity displays an intimate link to behaviour; engaging in a cognitive task produces a large reduction in the alpha/beta power (amplitude squared).
evidence: This is stated as an established phenomenon in the introduction.

claim: Task-induced alpha/beta power decreases can be observed across species including humans, macaques, rodents and cats.
source: These task-induced power decreases are ubiquitous, and can be observed across species (including humans [Pfurtscheller et al., 1994], macaques [Haegens et al., 2011], rodents [Wiest and Nicolelis, 2003] and cats [Chatila et al., 1992])
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations supporting the cross-species observation.

claim: Task-induced alpha/beta power decreases can be observed across sensory modalities including visual, auditory, and somatosensory domains.
source: sensory modalities (including visual [Pfurtscheller et al., 1994], auditory [Krause et al., 1994], and somatosensory [Crone et al., 1998] domains)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations supporting the cross-modality observation.

claim: Task-induced alpha/beta power decreases can be observed across cognitive tasks including perception, memory formation/retrieval, and language processing.
source: cognitive tasks (including perception [Pfurtscheller et al., 1994; Krause et al., 1994; Crone et al., 1998], memory formation/retrieval [Griffiths et al., 2016; Hanslmayr et al., 2009; Waldhauser et al., 2016], and language processing [Obleser and Weisz, 2012])
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations supporting the cross-task observation.

claim: Alpha/beta power decreases reflect a highly general brain process.
source: Given their ubiquity, it stands to reason that these decreases reflect a highly general brain process.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the introduction based on the ubiquity of the phenomenon.

claim: Alpha/beta power decreases are a proxy for information processing.
source: we provide empirical evidence in support of a new perspective: alpha/beta power decreases are a proxy for information processing.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the paper stated in the introduction.

claim: The brain must be capable of elevating the signal of a stimulus above the noise generated by ongoing neuronal activity to successfully process information about that stimulus.
source: To successfully process information about a stimulus, the brain must be capable of elevating the signal of said stimulus above the noise generated by ongoing neuronal activity (Harris and Thiele, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical principle in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Mass synchronised spiking is problematic when the ongoing spiking of a large population of neurons is correlated.
source: In situations where the ongoing spiking of a large population of neurons is correlated, this is problematic (Averbeck et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation supporting the claim.

claim: Mass synchronised spiking generates noise that conceals the comparatively small neuronal signal evoked by the stimulus.
source: Mass synchronised spiking generates noise that conceals the comparatively small neuronal signal evoked by the stimulus (see Figure 1a)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: Mass synchronised spiking renders momentary changes in sensory input undetectable.
source: Mass synchronised spiking generates noise that conceals the comparatively small neuronal signal evoked by the stimulus (see Figure 1a), rendering momentary changes in sensory input undetectable (Busch et al., 2009)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation supporting the claim.

claim: Mass synchronised spiking makes responses to temporally-extended changes unreliable.
source: rendering momentary changes in sensory input undetectable (Busch et al., 2009) and responses to temporally-extended changes unreliable (Goard and Dan, 2009)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation supporting the claim.

claim: Reducing neuronal noise correlations can boost the signal-to-noise ratio of an evoked neuronal response to a stimulus.
source: Reducing these neuronal 'noise correlations', therefore, can boost the signal-to-noise ratio of an evoked neuronal response to a stimulus.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical principle in the introduction.

claim: The decorrelation of task-irrelevant neuronal firing accompanies engagement in cognitive tasks.
source: Indeed, numerous studies have demonstrated that the decorrelation of task-irrelevant neuronal firing accompanies engagement in cognitive tasks (Goard and Dan, 2009; Poulet and Petersen, 2008; Mitchell et al., 2009; Churchland et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: Noise correlations show a strong positive correlation with the local field potential (LFP).
source: Given that these noise correlations show a strong positive correlation with the local field potential (LFP) (Cui et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation supporting the claim.

claim: Task-induced reductions in alpha/beta LFP are (to some degree) a marker of the reduction of noise correlations.
source: one may speculate that task-induced reductions in alpha/beta LFP (Haegens et al., 2011 ) are (to some degree) a marker of the reduction of noise correlations.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Reductions in alpha/beta power are associated with the successful execution of a wide range of cognitive tasks, from visual perception to memory retrieval.
source: Such a hypothesis would explain why reductions in alpha/beta power are associated with the successful execution of a wide range of cognitive tasks, from visual perception (Pfurtscheller et al., 1994) to memory retrieval (Michelmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations supporting the claim.

claim: Participants were presented with one of four videos (and on alternating blocks, one of four melodies), followed by a noun, and asked to pair the two.
source: On each trial, participants were presented with one of four videos (and on alternating blocks, one of four melodies), followed by a noun, and asked to pair the two.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure stated in the introduction.

claim: Participants were presented with the noun and asked to recall the associated video/melody, which would lead to the reinstatement of stimulus-specific information about the video/melody.
source: Later, participants were presented with the noun and asked to recall the associated video/melody (which would lead to the reinstatement of stimulus-specific information about the video/melody; Staresina et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure stated in the introduction with a citation supporting the concept of reinstatement.

claim: Representational similarity analysis (RSA) on fMRI data was used to quantify the relative distance between neural patterns of matching and differing videos/melodies.
source: We first conducted representational similarity analysis (RSA) on the acquired fMRI data to quantify the relative distance between neural patterns of matching and differing videos/melodies.
evidence: This is a description of the analytical method stated in the introduction.

claim: RSA provides a data-driven and objective measure of stimulus-specific information present during a single trial.
source: This provides a data-driven and objective measure of stimulus-specific information present during a single trial.
evidence: This is stated as a characterization of the RSA method in the introduction.

claim: Post-stimulus alpha/beta power decreases negatively correlated with the amount of stimulus-specific information observed in the cortex.
source: Foreshadowing the results reported below, we found that post-stimulus alpha/beta power decreases negatively correlated with the amount of stimulus-specific information observed in the cortex.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding stated in the introduction.

claim: Evidence for the negative correlation between alpha/beta power and stimulus-specific information was found during both the perception and retrieval of videos, as well as during the perception of melodies.
source: Importantly, we find evidence for this during both the perception and retrieval of these videos, as well as during the perception of the melodies, providing conceptual replication of our results and supporting the modality- and task-general nature of our hypothesis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a summary of findings across conditions.

claim: During visual perception, whole-brain searchlight analysis revealed a significant increase in stimulus-specific information relative to chance bilaterally in the occipital lobe (pFWE <0.001, k = 9911, peak MNI: [x = −30, y = −57, z = −2], Cohen's dz = 1.79).
source: During visual perception, whole-brain searchlight analysis revealed a significant increase in stimulus-specific information relative to chance bilaterally in the occipital lobe (pFWE <0.001, k = 9911, peak MNI: [x = −30, y = −57, z = −2], Cohen's dz = 1.79) [see Figure 2a].
evidence: This is a specific result from the fMRI analysis reported in the Results section with statistical details and reference to Figure 2a.

claim: The occipital lobe is critical in the representation of dynamically-unfolding visual information.
source: This corroborates the findings of numerous early studies (for example Chen et al., 2017; Baldassano et al., 2017) which indicate that the occipital lobe is critical in the representation of dynamically-unfolding visual information.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations supporting the claim.

claim: A frontal central cluster (pFWE <0.001, k = 113, peak MNI: [x = 12, y = −16, z = 50], Cohen's dz = 0.28) was uncovered during visual perception.
source: A frontal central cluster (pFWE <0.001, k = 113, peak MNI: [x = 12, y = −16, z = 50], Cohen's dz = 0.28) and a left temporal cluster (pFWE = 0.003, k = 64, peak MNI: [x = −48, y = −1, z = 18], Cohen's dz = 0.81) were also uncovered.
evidence: This is a specific result from the fMRI analysis reported in the Results section with statistical details.

claim: A left temporal cluster (pFWE = 0.003, k = 64, peak MNI: [x = −48, y = −1, z = 18], Cohen's dz = 0.81) was uncovered during visual perception.
source: A frontal central cluster (pFWE <0.001, k = 113, peak MNI: [x = 12, y = −16, z = 50], Cohen's dz = 0.28) and a left temporal cluster (pFWE = 0.003, k = 64, peak MNI: [x = −48, y = −1, z = 18], Cohen's dz = 0.81) were also uncovered.
evidence: This is a specific result from the fMRI analysis reported in the Results section with statistical details.

claim: The frontal central cluster may reflect goal-directed tracking of the visual stimulus.
source: The former may reflect goal-directed tracking of the visual stimulus (Holroyd et al., 2018)
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: The left temporal cluster may reflect high-level semantic representations of the stimulus.
source: while the latter may reflect high-level semantic representations of the stimulus (Visser et al., 2010; Rice et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Results section with citations.

claim: During auditory perception, whole-brain searchlight analysis revealed a significant increase in stimulus-specific information relative to chance bilaterally in the temporal lobe (left temporal: pFWE <0.001, k = 698, peak MNI: [x = −57, y = −37, z = 10], Cohen's dz = 0.86; right temporal: pFWE <0.001, k = 859, peak MNI: [x = 60, y = −25, z = 10], Cohen's dz = 1.20).
source: During auditory perception, whole-brain searchlight analysis revealed a significant increase in stimulus-specific information relative to chance bilaterally in the temporal lobe (left temporal: pFWE <0.001, k = 698, peak MNI: [x = −57, y = −37, z = 10], Cohen's dz = 0.86; right temporal: pFWE <0.001, k = 859, peak MNI: [x = 60, y = −25, z = 10], Cohen's dz = 1.20) [see Figure 2b].
evidence: This is a specific result from the fMRI analysis reported in the Results section with statistical details and reference to Figure 2b.

claim: Stimulus-specific information is represented within the cortex during both visual and auditory perception.
source: These results demonstrate that stimulus-specific information is represented within the cortex during both visual and auditory perception
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the fMRI findings.

claim: During visual memory retrieval, whole-brain searchlight analysis revealed a significant increase in reinstated stimulus-specific information relative to chance in the right fusiform gyrus (pFWE <0.001, k = 313, peak MNI: [x = 30, y = −46, z = −14], Cohen's dz = 1.07) and left fusiform gyrus (pFWE <0.001, k = 456, peak MNI: [x = −45, y = −37, z = −6], Cohen's dz = 0.69).
source: During visual memory retrieval, whole-brain searchlight analysis revealed a significant increase in reinstated stimulus-specific information relative to chance in the right fusiform gyrus (pFWE <0.001, k = 313, peak MNI: [x = 30, y = −46, z = −14], Cohen's dz = 1.07) and left fusiform gyrus (pFWE <0.001, k = 456, peak MNI: [x = −45, y = −37, z = −6], Cohen's dz = 0.69) [see Figure 2c].
evidence: This is a specific result from the fMRI analysis reported in the Results section with statistical details and reference to Figure 2c.

claim: The reinstatement effect during visual memory retrieval was not driven by the presentation of video stills that followed the presentation of the retrieval cue.
source: Notably, this effect was not driven by the presentation of video stills that followed the presentation of the retrieval cue (see Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: Stimulus-specific information is reinstated during the retrieval of visual information.
source: These results demonstrate that stimulus-specific information is reinstated during the retrieval of visual information
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the fMRI findings.

claim: No significant cluster was identified during auditory memory retrieval (left frontal cluster: pFWE = 0.153, k = 28, peak MNI: [x = −39, y = 44, z = 14], Cohen's dz = 0.36).
source: No significant cluster was identified during auditory memory retrieval (left frontal cluster: pFWE = 0.153, k = 28, peak MNI: [x = −39, y = 44, z = 14], Cohen's dz = 0.36; see Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a specific result from the fMRI analysis reported in the Results section with statistical details.

claim: Memory performance was substantially worse for the auditory stimuli (52.9%) when compared to visual stimuli (73.8%; t(20) = 7.13, p<0.001).
source: It is unclear why we could not find evidence for retrieved auditory information, but it may be explained by the fact that memory performance was substantially worse for the auditory stimuli (52.9%) when compared to visual stimuli (73.8%; t(20) = 7.13, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a specific behavioral result reported in the Results section with statistical details.

claim: Poor memory performance for auditory stimuli meant that fewer trials could be included in the similarity analysis, limiting the statistical power of the analysis.
source: Poor memory performance meant that fewer trials could be included in the similarity analysis, limiting the statistical power of the analysis.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Results section explaining the null finding.

claim: A significant decrease in alpha/beta power was found following visual stimulus presentation (p<0.001, Cohen's dz = 0.95).
source: We found a significant decrease in alpha/beta power following visual stimulus presentation (p<0.001, Cohen's dz = 0.95; see Figure 3a–d)
evidence: This is a specific result from the EEG analysis reported in the Results section with statistical details and reference to Figure 3.

claim: Power decreases evoked by the visual stimuli were predominately observed in the occipital lobe.
source: Power decreases evoked by the visual stimuli were predominately observed in the occipital lobe, while power decreases evoked by the auditory stimuli were observed in the parietal and temporal lobes (see Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a specific result from the EEG analysis reported in the Results section with reference to Figure 3d.

claim: Power decreases evoked by the auditory stimuli were observed in the parietal and temporal lobes.
source: Power decreases evoked by the visual stimuli were predominately observed in the occipital lobe, while power decreases evoked by the auditory stimuli were observed in the parietal and temporal lobes (see Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a specific result from the EEG analysis reported in the Results section with reference to Figure 3d.

claim: A significant reduction in alpha/beta power was found for recalled pairs, relative to forgotten pairs (p=0.017, Cohen's dz = 0.56).
source: Matching earlier reports, we found a significant reduction in alpha/beta power for recalled pairs, relative to forgotten pairs (p=0.017, Cohen's dz = 0.56; see Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a specific result from the EEG analysis reported in the Results section with statistical details and reference to figures.

claim: Power decreases for recalled vs. forgotten pairs were localised to the late visual ventral stream (including the region within the fusiform gyrus where stimulus-specific information could be identified), as well as other parts of the memory network (including the medial temporal lobe and medial prefrontal cortex).
source: These power decreases were localised to the late visual ventral stream (including the region within the fusiform gyrus where stimulus-specific information could be identified), as well as other parts of the memory network (Rugg and Vilberg, 2013) (including the medial temporal lobe and medial prefrontal cortex; see Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a specific result from the EEG analysis reported in the Results section with a citation and reference to Figure 3d.

claim: No region exhibited an increase in alpha/beta power during the 500-1500 ms post-stimulus window.
source: No region exhibited an increase in alpha/beta power during this window.
evidence: This is a specific result from the EEG analysis reported in the Results section.

claim: During visual perception, a trending negative correlation was found between alpha/beta power and stimulus-specific information (p=0.054, Cohen's dz = 0.34).
source: During visual perception, we found a trending negative correlation (p=0.054, Cohen's dz = 0.34), where a reduction in alpha/beta power was accompanied by an increase in stimulus-specific information (see Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a specific result from the combined EEG-fMRI analysis reported in the Results section with statistical details and reference to Figure 4b.

claim: During visual perception, a reduction in alpha/beta power was accompanied by an increase in stimulus-specific information.
source: During visual perception, we found a trending negative correlation (p=0.054, Cohen's dz = 0.34), where a reduction in alpha/beta power was accompanied by an increase in stimulus-specific information (see Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a specific result from the combined EEG-fMRI analysis reported in the Results section.

claim: During visual perception, BOLD amplitude, confidence rating, and pre-stimulus alpha/beta power did not correlate with stimulus-specific information.
source: The additional regressors did not correlate with stimulus-specific information (see Figure 4e; BOLD amplitude: p=0.917, Cohen's dz = 0.02; confidence rating: p=0.736, Cohen's dz = 0.07; pre-stimulus alpha/beta power: p=0.141, Cohen's dz = 0.34).
evidence: This is a specific result from the combined EEG-fMRI analysis reported in the Results section with statistical details.

claim: During auditory perception, a significant negative correlation was found between alpha/beta power and stimulus-specific information (p=0.006, Cohen's dz = 0.56).
source: During auditory perception, we found a larger, significant negative correlation (p=0.006, Cohen's dz = 0.56), where a reduction in alpha/beta power was accompanied by an increase in stimulus-specific information (see Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a specific result from the combined EEG-fMRI analysis reported in the Results section with statistical details and reference to Figure 4b.

claim: During auditory perception, a reduction in alpha/beta power was accompanied by an increase in stimulus-specific information.
source: During auditory perception, we found a larger, significant negative correlation (p=0.006, Cohen's dz = 0.56), where a reduction in alpha/beta power was accompanied by an increase in stimulus-specific information (see Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a specific result from the combined EEG-fMRI analysis reported in the Results section.

claim: During auditory perception, BOLD amplitude and pre-stimulus power did not correlate with stimulus-specific information.
source: Neither BOLD amplitude (p=0.311, Cohen's dz = 0.23) nor pre-stimulus power (p=0.123, Cohen's dz = 0.34), correlated with the stimulus-specific information
evidence: This is a specific result from the combined EEG-fMRI analysis reported in the Results section with statistical details.

claim: During auditory perception, confidence rating correlated with stimulus-specific information (p=0.031, Cohen's dz = 0.47).
source: though confidence rating did (p=0.031, Cohen's dz = 0.47).
evidence: This is a specific result from the combined EEG-fMRI analysis reported in the Results section with statistical details.

claim: Post-stimulus alpha/beta power decreases correlate with an increase in perceived stimulus-specific information.
source: These results indicate that post-stimulus alpha/beta power decreases correlate with an increase in perceived stimulus-specific information.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the combined EEG-fMRI findings.

claim: During visual memory retrieval, a significant negative correlation was found between alpha/beta power and stimulus-specific information for remembered trials (p<0.001, Cohen's dz = 0.56).
source: In line with the previous results, we found a significant negative correlation for remembered trials (p<0.001, Cohen's dz = 0.56), where a reduction in post-stimulus alpha/beta power was accompanied by an increase in stimulus-specific information (see Figure 4b–d).
evidence: This is a specific result from the combined EEG-fMRI analysis reported in the Results section with statistical details and reference to Figure 4.

claim: During visual memory retrieval, a reduction in post-stimulus alpha/beta power was accompanied by an increase in stimulus-specific information.
source: In line with the previous results, we found a significant negative correlation for remembered trials (p<0.001, Cohen's dz = 0.56), where a reduction in post-stimulus alpha/beta power was accompanied by an increase in stimulus-specific information (see Figure 4b–d).
evidence: This is a specific result from the combined EEG-fMRI analysis reported in the Results section.

claim: During visual memory retrieval, BOLD amplitude, confidence rating, and pre-stimulus alpha/beta power did not correlate with stimulus-specific information.
source: The additional regressors did not correlate with stimulus-specific information (BOLD amplitude: p=0.598, Cohen's dz = 0.12; confidence rating: p=0.798, Cohen's dz = 0.06; pre-stimulus alpha/beta power: p=0.204, Cohen's dz = 0.30).
evidence: This is a specific result from the combined EEG-fMRI analysis reported in the Results section with statistical details.

claim: Event-related decreases in power are a summation of decreases in oscillatory alpha/beta power and changes in the shape of the 1/f curve.
source: In line with these ideas, we found that event-related decreases in power are a summation of decreases in oscillatory alpha/beta power and changes in the shape of the 1/f curve (see Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a specific result from the IRASA analysis reported in the Results section with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: Memory-related power changes were only reflected in decreases in alpha/beta oscillatory signal.
source: Interestingly however, memory-related power changes were only reflected in decreases in alpha/beta oscillatory signal.
evidence: This is a specific result from the IRASA analysis reported in the Results section.

claim: Alpha/beta power parametrically decreases as the amount of stimulus-specific information represented within the cortex increases.
source: In sum, these results suggest that alpha/beta power parametrically decreases as the amount of stimulus-specific information represented within the cortex increases.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the Results section based on the combined findings.

claim: Cluster-based, permutation t-test found no evidence to suggest that alpha/beta power represents stimulus-specific information during visual perception (p=0.548, Cohen's dz = 0.03).
source: Despite this extremely liberal approach, a cluster-based, permutation t-test found no evidence to suggest that alpha/beta power represents stimulus-specific information during visual perception (p=0.548, Cohen's dz = 0.03)
evidence: This is a specific result from the EEG RSA analysis reported in the Results section with statistical details.

claim: Cluster-based, permutation t-test found no evidence to suggest that alpha/beta power represents stimulus-specific information during auditory perception (p=0.773, Cohen's dz = 0.17).
source: a cluster-based, permutation t-test found no evidence to suggest that alpha/beta power represents stimulus-specific information during visual perception (p=0.548, Cohen's dz = 0.03), auditory perception (p=0.773, Cohen's dz = 0.17)
evidence: This is a specific result from the EEG RSA analysis reported in the Results section with statistical details.

claim: Cluster-based, permutation t-test found no evidence to suggest that alpha/beta power represents stimulus-specific information during visual retrieval (p=0.579, Cohen's dz = 0.04).
source: a cluster-based, permutation t-test found no evidence to suggest that alpha/beta power represents stimulus-specific information during visual perception (p=0.548, Cohen's dz = 0.03), auditory perception (p=0.773, Cohen's dz = 0.17) or visual retrieval (p=0.579, Cohen's dz = 0.04).
evidence: This is a specific result from the EEG RSA analysis reported in the Results section with statistical details.

claim: Bayesian one-sample t-tests revealed moderate evidence in favour of the null hypothesis for the visual perceptual task (BF10 = 0.230).
source: Bayesian one-sample t-tests revealed moderate evidence in favour of the null hypothesis for the visual perceptual (BF10 = 0.230), auditory perceptual (BF10 = 0.272), and visual retrieval tasks (BF10 = 0.232).
evidence: This is a specific result from the Bayesian analysis reported in the Results section with statistical details.

claim: Bayesian one-sample t-tests revealed moderate evidence in favour of the null hypothesis for the auditory perceptual task (BF10 = 0.272).
source: Bayesian one-sample t-tests revealed moderate evidence in favour of the null hypothesis for the visual perceptual (BF10 = 0.230), auditory perceptual (BF10 = 0.272), and visual retrieval tasks (BF10 = 0.232).
evidence: This is a specific result from the Bayesian analysis reported in the Results section with statistical details.

claim: Bayesian one-sample t-tests revealed moderate evidence in favour of the null hypothesis for the visual retrieval task (BF10 = 0.232).
source: Bayesian one-sample t-tests revealed moderate evidence in favour of the null hypothesis for the visual perceptual (BF10 = 0.230), auditory perceptual (BF10 = 0.272), and visual retrieval tasks (BF10 = 0.232).
evidence: This is a specific result from the Bayesian analysis reported in the Results section with statistical details.

claim: The observed relationship between alpha/beta power decreases and stimulus-specific information cannot be explained by the hypothesis that alpha/beta power itself represents information.
source: These results suggest that the observed relationship between alpha/beta power decreases and stimulus-specific information cannot be explained by the hypothesis that alpha/beta power itself represents information.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the RSA and Bayesian analyses.

claim: Alpha/beta power decreases are a marker of the fidelity of stimulus-specific information.
source: Rather these results suggest that alpha/beta power decreases are a marker of the fidelity of stimulus-specific information.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the combined findings.

claim: Task-induced alpha/beta power decreases track the fidelity of stimulus-specific information represented within the cortex.
source: Here, we provide empirical evidence to suggest that task-induced alpha/beta power decreases track the fidelity of stimulus-specific information represented within the cortex.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the Discussion section.

claim: As stimulus-specific information increased, alpha/beta power decreased, regardless of whether the information was externally presented or internally generated, or whether the information was visual or auditory.
source: As stimulus-specific information increased, alpha/beta power decreased, regardless of whether the information was externally presented or internally generated, or whether the information was visual or auditory.
evidence: This is a summary of findings stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The effect of alpha/beta power decreases tracking stimulus-specific information is not driven by the fact that alpha/beta power decreases represent information.
source: Further analysis revealed that this effect is not driven by the fact that alpha/beta power decreases represent information, suggesting instead that these decreases provide conditions which are beneficial for information processing.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the RSA analysis results.

claim: Alpha/beta power decreases provide conditions which are beneficial for information processing.
source: Further analysis revealed that this effect is not driven by the fact that alpha/beta power decreases represent information, suggesting instead that these decreases provide conditions which are beneficial for information processing.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Alpha/beta power decreases may mark information processing as they allow for a reduction of neuronal noise correlations.
source: Mechanistically speaking, these decreases may mark information processing as they allow for a reduction of neuronal noise correlations (which map onto local field potential; LFP; Cui et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation stated in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: Task-irrelevant correlated activity between pairs of neurons is detrimental to stimulus processing.
source: Numerous studies have demonstrated that task-irrelevant correlated activity between pairs of neurons is detrimental to stimulus processing (Harris and Thiele, 2011; Zohary et al., 1994)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations supporting the claim.

claim: Large networks of correlated neurons are more likely to be detected in the LFP.
source: particularly for large networks of correlated neurons (Averbeck et al., 2006) that, incidentally, are more likely to be detected in the LFP.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: Alpha/beta power decreases do not carry any stimulus-specific information during the perception or retrieval of the visual stimuli.
source: In line with this hypothesis, we found moderate evidence to suggest that alpha/beta power decreases do not carry any stimulus-specific information during the perception or retrieval of the visual stimuli.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the Bayesian analysis results.

claim: The power and phase of an oscillation are mathematically independent.
source: As the power and phase of an oscillation are mathematically independent, it is entirely plausible to suggest that one carries stimulus-specific information while the other does not.
evidence: This is stated as a mathematical fact in the Discussion section.

claim: Alpha/beta power decreases can be viewed as a marker for the potential for information processing, rather than representing information.
source: As such, one could view alpha/beta power decreases as a marker for the potential for information processing, rather than representing information.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Information theory proposes that little information can be gathered from a highly predictable input.
source: Information theory proposes that little information can be gathered from a highly predictable input (e.g. a network of highly correlated, spiking neurons) – if you can predict an upcoming event, you must already know details about the event.
evidence: This is stated as a principle from information theory in the Discussion section.

claim: A lot of information can be gathered from unpredictable inputs.
source: In contrast, a lot of information can be gathered from unpredictable inputs (e.g. uncorrelated spiking neurons) – you learn a lot from a completely novel experience.
evidence: This is stated as a principle from information theory in the Discussion section.

claim: Desynchronisation within the alpha and beta bands reduces the predictability of neuronal firing and hence boosts information processing abilities.
source: It has been theorised that desynchronisation within the alpha and beta bands reduces the predictability of neuronal firing and hence boosts information processing abilities (Hanslmayr et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: Tasks which involve greater semantic elaboration produce greater alpha/beta power decreases.
source: For example, earlier work has demonstrated that tasks which involve greater semantic elaboration (i.e. greater information processing) produce greater alpha/beta power decreases (Hanslmayr et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: Alpha/beta power decreases allow for the rich representation of stimulus-specific information by reducing the predictability of neural firing patterns.
source: Taken together, one could speculate that alpha/beta power decreases allow for the rich representation of stimulus-specific information by reducing the predictability of neural firing patterns.
evidence: This is stated as speculation in the Discussion section.

claim: High-amplitude alpha oscillations are a marker for inhibition.
source: Several established accounts have interpreted high-amplitude alpha oscillations as a marker for inhibition (Pfurtscheller et al., 1996; Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010; Klimesch et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations.

claim: The information processing account and the existing inhibition accounts are two sides of the same coin.
source: Quite simply, we view the information processing account and the existing inhibition accounts as two sides of the same coin.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Alpha/beta power can parametrically track the degree to which a network can represent information.
source: Importantly, we expand on these earlier accounts by demonstrating that alpha/beta power does not simply reflect a binary division between inhibition and disinhibition. Rather, alpha/beta power can parametrically track the degree to which a network can represent information.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an expansion of previous theories.

claim: As alpha/beta power gets progressively weaker, the network becomes progressively disinhibited and more capable of establishing detailed neural representations.
source: In other words, as alpha/beta power gets progressively weaker, the network becomes progressively disinhibited and, therefore, more capable of establishing detailed neural representations.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Discussion section.

claim: A decrease in pre-stimulus alpha power correlates with an increase in perceptual performance.
source: This presents an apparent contradiction to earlier work which has shown that a decrease in pre-stimulus alpha power correlates with an increase in perceptual performance (van Dijk et al., 2008; Hanslmayr et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations.

claim: The link between pre-stimulus alpha power and perceptual performance can be better explained by decision criterion rather than by sensitivity.
source: A potential resolution to this peculiarity lies in a number of recent studies (Wöstmann et al., 2019; Iemi et al., 2017; Lange et al., 2013; Samaha et al., 2017; Limbach and Corballis, 2016; Benwell et al., 2017; Whitmarsh et al., 2017) which have used signal detection theory (Green and Swets, 1966) to disentangle objective and subjective measures of perceptual performance (termed 'sensitivity' and 'decision criterion' respectively). These studies demonstrate that the link between pre-stimulus alpha power and perceptual performance can be better explained by decision criterion (e.g. increases in responses rates; confidence; awareness) rather than by sensitivity (e.g. increased task accuracy).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with multiple citations.

claim: Pre-stimulus power does not correlate with measures of sensitivity.
source: As these previous studies have demonstrated consistently that pre-stimulus power does not correlate with measures of sensitivity, it is perhaps no surprise that we found no correlation between stimulus-specific information and pre-stimulus power.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on previous literature.

claim: Stimulus-induced reductions in alpha/beta power are more complicated than a simple reduction in oscillatory power.
source: In our EEG analyses, we demonstrated that stimulus-induced reductions in alpha/beta power are a summation of decreases in alpha/beta oscillatory activity, a flattening of the 1/f curve, and an overall increase in power. These results suggest that stimulus-induced decreases in alpha/beta power are more complicated than a simple reduction in oscillatory power.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the IRASA analysis results.

claim: The 1/f curve cannot explain memory-related changes in power.
source: Intriguingly, memory-related change in alpha/beta activity could only be explained by a decrease in alpha/beta oscillatory power (confirming earlier findings which suggest that the 1/f curve cannot explain memory-related changes in power; Fellner et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: The 1/f curve cannot be properly estimated for single-trial, event-related analyses.
source: It is unclear why this occurred, but one plausible explanation is that the 1/f curve cannot be properly estimated for single-trial, event-related analyses.
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation in the Discussion section.

claim: The 1/f slope is a product of many seconds of recorded signal and cannot be estimated 'instanteously'.
source: As the 1/f slope is a product of many seconds of recorded signal, it cannot be estimated 'instanteously' (Miller et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: Short epochs (<5 s) give unreliable estimates of the 1/f curve.
source: Supplementary simulations (see Figure 4—figure supplement 5) demonstrate this. Short epochs (<5 s) give unreliable estimates of the 1/f curve, but these estimates stabilise as epoch length increases (>20 s) or when epochs are averaged together.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to a supplementary figure showing simulation results.

claim: The correlation between alpha/beta power decreases and stimulus-specific information was weakest during visual perception.
source: Intriguingly, our analysis revealed that the correlation between alpha/beta power decreases and stimulus-specific information was weakest during visual perception.
evidence: This is an observation stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The comparatively small effect in the visual perception task relative to the auditory perception and memory retrieval tasks may be explained by a limited variation in stimulus representation across trials.
source: In short, the comparatively small effect in the visual perception task relative to the auditory perception and memory retrieval tasks may be explained by a limited variation in stimulus representation across trials.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Alpha/beta power decreases are sufficient, though not necessary, for information processing.
source: Arguably however, the stimulus's signal-to-noise ratio can also be boosted by increasing the stimulus's signal intensity (Fries, 2015). This would lead us to hypothesise that alpha/beta power decreases are sufficient, though not necessary, for information processing.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: TMS reduced behavioural performance when task-related alpha/beta power decreases were disrupted.
source: Indeed, this hypothesis is supported by a study where task-related alpha/beta power decreases were disrupted by transcranial magnetic stimulation (Waldhauser et al., 2016) (TMS). In this study, TMS reduced behavioural performance (suggesting that task-related alpha/beta power decreases facilitate information processing)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: TMS did not render participants completely incapable of recalling information when task-related alpha/beta power decreases were disrupted.
source: but did not render participants completely incapable of recalling information (suggesting other processes also contribute to information processing).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the cited TMS study.

claim: The perception and retrieval of stimuli typically induce power increases in the theta and gamma bands.
source: Both the perception and retrieval of stimuli typically induce power increases in the theta and gamma bands (for example Jutras et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: Theta or gamma power increases could theoretically facilitate information processing through the complementary means of increasing signal strength.
source: As alpha/beta power decreases are proposed to facilitate information processing by reducing noise, however, these theta or gamma power increases could theoretically facilitate information processing through the complementary means of increasing signal strength.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical possibility in the Discussion section.

claim: The 'communication through coherence' hypothesis proposes that neuronal representations of a stimulus are enhanced by an increase in gamma synchronicity.
source: For example, the 'communication through coherence' hypothesis proposes that neuronal representations of a stimulus are enhanced by an increase in gamma synchronicity (Fries, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: Alpha/beta power decreases frequently co-occur with gamma power increases.
source: Given that alpha/beta power decreases frequently co-occur with gamma power increases (for example Burke et al., 2014)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: Alpha/beta power decreases and gamma power increases may interact such that the former reduces noise while the latter boosts signal to further optimise the efficiency of information processing.
source: one could speculate that these two mechanisms interact such that the former reduces noise while the latter boosts signal to further optimise the efficiency of information processing.
evidence: This is stated as speculation in the Discussion section.

claim: Thirty-three participants were recruited for the study.
source: Thirty-three participants were recruited.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Twelve participants were excluded from analysis.
source: Twelve of these participants were excluded from analysis: one participant was excluded due to recording issues relating to the MRI scanner, three participants were excluded due to recording issues relating to the EEG system, five participants had insufficient recalled pairs (n < 10) following EEG artifact rejection, and three participants had insufficient forgotten pairs (n < 10) following EEG artifact rejection.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Participants correctly recalled 63.4% of the video-word pairs on average (s.d. 7.5%; range: 47.6–74.5%).
source: Under these criteria, participants (on average) correctly recalled 63.4% of the video-word pairs (s.d. 7.5%; range: 47.6–74.5%).
evidence: This is a behavioral result stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The cross-validated Mahalanobis (CVM) distance provides an unbiased measure of pattern dissimilarity.
source: Representational distance was quantified as the cross-validated Mahalanobis (CVM) distance (Nili et al., 2014; Walther et al., 2016), which provides an unbiased measure of pattern dissimilarity (Walther et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with citations.

claim: Cluster-forming thresholding may inflate the family-wise error rate from the expected 5% to 7–10%.
source: Notably, such cluster-forming thresholding may inflate from family-wise error rate from the expected 5% to 7–10% (Eklund et al., 2016) and hence classify marginal effects as erroneously significant.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with a citation.

claim: A significant negative correlation was found between alpha/beta power and confidence rating (p=0.033, Cohen's d = 0.48).
source: We found a significant negative correlation (p=0.033, Cohen's d = 0.48), where a reduction in alpha/beta power was accompanied by an increase in confidence rating.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section under EEG-confidence correlation.

claim: The link between alpha/beta power and confidence does not explain the link between alpha/beta power and stimulus-specific information.
source: While these results indicate a link between alpha/beta power and confidence, this link does not explain the link between alpha/beta power and stimulus-specific information (as evidenced by the partial correlation reported in the results section).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.
